relearning.title: Read: free-body diagrams and net force
relearning.description: A short reading with the tug-of-war analogy, worked examples and quick checks.

body.text:
**I can calculate forces acting on an object using a free-body diagram (FBD).**

**Think of tug-of-war.** If both teams pull equally hard, the rope doesn't move: the pulls cancel. If one team pulls harder, the rope moves toward that team, and only the difference between the teams matters. Forces on an object work the same way.

**Rule 1.** An **FBD** shows only the forces acting on one object. Each arrow shows a force's direction, and its length shows the force's size.

**Rule 2.** Forces in the **same direction add**. Forces in **opposite directions subtract**, and the net force points toward the bigger side. Do horizontal and vertical forces separately.

**Rule 3.** **Type A:** the net force is 0 N (balanced), so the object is at rest or moving at a constant velocity. **Type B:** there is a net force (unbalanced), so the object speeds up, slows down, or changes direction.

**Worked example:** A wagon is pulled right with 70 N, and friction pulls left with 25 N. Formula: Fnet = Fapp − Ff. Set up: Fnet = 70 N − 25 N. Answer: **45 N to the right**, so the wagon speeds up (Type B).

checks.prompt: Two students push a desk to the right with 30 N and 15 N. Friction pushes left with 20 N. What is the net force? Type a number (in N).
checks.explanation: Add the forces that point the same way (30 N + 15 N = 45 N right), then subtract the one that points the other way: 45 N − 20 N = 25 N to the right. Adding all three (65 N) is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: A box sits at rest on the floor with Fg = 50 N down and FN = 50 N up. What is the net force on it?
checks.explanation: Opposite directions subtract: 50 N − 50 N = 0 N. That is Type A, so the box stays at rest. Adding them (100 N) is the common mistake.

sections.title: Arrow lengths and balanced forces

body.text:
**Arrow lengths tell the story.** Constant velocity: Fapp and Ff are the **same length**. Speeding up: Fapp is **longer** than Ff. Slowing down: Ff is longer, or there is no forward force at all (coasting). Falling and speeding up: Fg is longer than Fair.

**Normal force.** For an object at rest on a level surface, the normal force balances the weight: **FN = Fg = m × g**, with g = 9.8 m/s².

**Worked example 2:** A 10 kg box sits at rest on a level floor. What is the normal force? Formula: FN = Fg = m × g. Set up: FN = 10 kg × 9.8 m/s². Answer: **98 N up**.

**Worked example 3:** An 80 kg skydiver falls at a constant velocity. How big is the air resistance? Constant velocity means Type A, so Fair = Fg. Formula: Fair = m × g. Set up: Fair = 80 kg × 9.8 m/s². Answer: **784 N up**.

**Watch out for:** adding forces that point in opposite directions (20 N up and 20 N down is 0 N, not 40 N), drawing a longer forward arrow for constant velocity, giving a kicked ball a force from the kick after it leaves your foot, dividing by 9.8 when you should multiply, and mixing horizontal forces into the normal force.

checks.prompt: A 6 kg box of books sits at rest on a level floor. What is the normal force on it? Use g = 9.8 m/s². Type a number (in N).
checks.explanation: At rest on a level floor, FN = Fg = m × g = 6 kg × 9.8 m/s² = 58.8 N up. Dividing (6 ÷ 9.8 ≈ 0.61) is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: A falling ball has Fg = 6 N down and air resistance of 2 N up. What is the net force, and what does the ball do?

options.text: 4 N down; it falls at a constant velocity

checks.explanation: Opposite directions subtract: 6 N − 2 N = 4 N down. Fg is the longer arrow, so the net force points the way the ball moves and it speeds up (Type B). Adding the forces (8 N) is the common mistake, and a constant velocity would need Fg and Fair to be equal.

sections.shortAnswer: Explain how the Fapp and Ff arrows change between a car driving at a constant speed on Hwy 29 and the same car speeding up to merge.

relearning.title: Do: net force step by step
relearning.description: A net force problem one step at a time, then a balanced-forces problem.

sections.title: Worked problem: three forces on a box

body.problem: Two students push a box to the right with 55 N and 20 N. Friction pushes on the box 40 N to the left. Find the net force and tell what the box does.

steps.text: Sort the forces. Right: 55 N and 20 N. Left: friction, 40 N. Up and down, Fg and FN cancel, so only the sideways forces matter.
Same direction adds. Right: 55 N + 20 N = 75 N.
Opposite directions subtract. Fnet = 75 N − 40 N = 35 N.
The net force points toward the bigger side: 35 N to the right. There is a net force, so it is Type B: the box speeds up to the right.

checks.prompt: Your turn: a sled is pulled right with 90 N, and friction pulls left with 32 N. What is the net force? Type a number (in N).
checks.explanation: Opposite directions subtract: 90 N − 32 N = 58 N to the right. Adding them (122 N) is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: In tug-of-war, one team pulls left with 320 N and the other team pulls right with 320 N. What happens to the rope?

options.text: It moves with a net force of 640 N
Its motion doesn't change; the net force is 0 N

checks.explanation: Equal forces in opposite directions subtract to 0 N (Type A), so the rope's motion doesn't change. Adding them (640 N) is the common mistake.

sections.title: Worked problem: a skydiver at constant velocity

body.problem: A 65 kg skydiver falls at a constant velocity. How big is the air resistance on her? Use g = 9.8 m/s².

steps.text: Constant velocity means the motion is not changing, so the forces are balanced: Type A, net force = 0 N.
Draw the FBD: Fg points down, and Fair points up. Balanced means the arrows are the same length, so Fair = Fg.
Find her weight. Formula: Fg = m × g. Set up: Fg = 65 kg × 9.8 m/s². Answer: 637 N.
So the air resistance is 637 N up. If Fg were longer than Fair, she would still be speeding up.

checks.prompt: A wagon rolls along at a constant speed while a student pulls it with 40 N. How big is the friction on the wagon?
checks.explanation: Constant speed is Type A, so Fapp and Ff are the same length: friction is 40 N. Thinking the pull must be bigger than friction to keep the wagon moving is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: A 4 kg backpack sits at rest on a level desk, so FN balances Fg. What is the normal force? Use g = 9.8 m/s². Type a number (in N).
checks.explanation: At rest on a level surface is Type A, so FN = Fg = m × g = 4 kg × 9.8 m/s² = 39.2 N up. Dividing by 9.8 (about 0.41) is the common mistake.

relearning.title: U5.LT2 Watch: free-body diagrams and net force

checks.prompt: A box is pushed right with 50 N, and friction pushes left with 15 N. What is the net force? Type a number (in N).
checks.explanation: Opposite directions subtract: 50 N − 15 N = 35 N to the right, toward the bigger side. Adding them (65 N) is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: A car drives down the road at a constant velocity. What is true about the forces on it?

options.text: They are balanced: the net force is 0 N (Type A)
They are unbalanced: the forward force must be bigger than friction (Type B)
There are no forces on the car at all

checks.explanation: Constant velocity means the motion isn't changing, so the forces are balanced and the net force is 0 N (Type A). Thinking a moving object needs a bigger forward force to keep going is the common mistake.

sections.title: Forces and free-body diagrams

checks.prompt: On a free-body diagram, how do you show that one force is bigger than another?

options.text: Draw its arrow thicker but the same length

checks.explanation: Each arrow shows a force's direction, and its length shows the force's size, so a bigger force gets a longer arrow. Drawing every arrow the same length is the common mistake.

checks.prompt: A 12 kg box sits at rest on a level floor. What is the normal force on it? Use g = 9.8 m/s². Type a number (in N).
checks.explanation: At rest on a level floor, FN = Fg = m × g = 12 kg × 9.8 m/s² = 117.6 N up. Dividing (12 ÷ 9.8 ≈ 1.2) is the common mistake.

sections.shortAnswer: A sled is pulled to the right with 60 N while friction pulls left with 60 N. Describe its free-body diagram (which arrows, and how long) and tell whether it is Type A or Type B.
